Two questions came off the incident-command call and neither one has been
answered yet:

> "Why do last week's numbers keep changing *after* we've briefed them?"
>
> "And positivity is up — but I'm told most of our testing is rapid
> antigen now. Is that the same eleven percent it was in December?"

This chapter answers both from the lab feed, and adds what it finds to
the Situation Brief. The pattern is the one the last two chapters built:
**convert once, query many times.**

## Setup

Download the feed into your project the same way you did the town file —
it goes in `data/raw/`. The [Data Library](../data-library/index.qmd) has
the link.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| eval: false
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(arrow)
library(fs)
library(lubridate)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)
```

## Step 1 — Hoist the constants

Two things belong at the top: the paths, and the codes. Burying
`"260373001"` in the middle of a pipeline is how you end up with a
positivity rate nobody can check.

```{r}
#| label: constants
#| eval: false
RAW_CSV <- here("data", "raw", "synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv")
LAB_DATASET <- here("data", "processed", "lab-results")

# SNOMED CT concept ids for a positive result. "Detected" is what an
# amplification test reports; "Positive" is what serology reports.
POSITIVE_CODES <- c("260373001", "10828004")
```

```{r}
#| label: constants-book
#| include: false
# The book renders against its own shared data folder and a temp directory
# rather than your project — the code is otherwise identical.
RAW_CSV <- book_data_path("synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv")
LAB_DATASET <- path(tempdir(), "lab-results")
POSITIVE_CODES <- c("260373001", "10828004")
```

## Step 2 — Convert once

This is the step that only runs when new data arrives. Read the CSV,
fix the types **once**, add the partition columns, and write the dataset.

```{r}
#| label: convert
convert_feed <- function(csv_path, dataset_path) {
  # Convert the raw ELR csv export into a partitioned parquet dataset.
  #
  # csv_path: string - path to the raw csv from the lab feed
  # dataset_path: string - directory to write the parquet dataset into
  # Returns: the dataset path, invisibly

  raw <-
    read_csv(
      csv_path,
      col_types = cols(
        # Identifiers are labels, not numbers - say so here and the
        # parquet file remembers it forever.
        result_snomed = col_character(),
        specimen_source_snomed = col_character(),
        ordering_provider_npi = col_character(),
        patient_zip = col_character(),
        .default = col_guess()
      )
    )

  raw |>
    mutate(
      # Lab names arrive in mixed case from some senders. Normalize now,
      # so every later group_by() lands on one row per lab.
      performing_lab = str_to_title(performing_lab),
      collection_year = year(specimen_collection_dt),
      collection_month = month(specimen_collection_dt)
    ) |>
    write_dataset(
      path = dataset_path,
      format = "parquet",
      partitioning = c("collection_year", "collection_month")
    )

  invisible(dataset_path)
}

convert_feed(RAW_CSV, LAB_DATASET)

dir_ls(LAB_DATASET) |> path_file()
```

From here on, nothing reads the CSV again:

```{r}
#| label: open
lab_ds <- open_dataset(LAB_DATASET)

nrow(lab_ds)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Why this is a function and not five loose lines

Conversion is the one step in this analysis that will be run on a
schedule by someone who is not you — next month's extract, next quarter's
extract. Everything the conversion decides (which columns are
identifiers, how lab names are normalized, how the data is partitioned)
has to be decided the *same way* every time, or the dataset quietly
becomes two datasets. That's what a function is for.
:::

## Step 3 — Why the numbers keep changing, part one: lag

A result is not available the moment the swab is taken. The gap between
`specimen_collection_dt` and `result_dt` is the **turnaround time**, and
it is the reason a count for last Tuesday keeps going up after Tuesday.

```{r}
#| label: turnaround
turnaround <-
  lab_ds |>
  filter(!is.na(specimen_collection_dt)) |>
  mutate(
    # arrow returns a duration here, which it cannot convert with
    # as.numeric() - cast it to a plain integer instead.
    turnaround_secs = cast(
      difftime(result_dt, specimen_collection_dt, units = "secs"),
      int64()
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(collection_year, collection_month) |>
  summarise(
    tests = n(),
    median_secs = median(turnaround_secs),
    pct_over_3_days = 100 * mean(turnaround_secs > 3 * 86400),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(
    month = make_date(collection_year, collection_month, 1),
    median_days = round(median_secs / 86400, 1),
    pct_over_3_days = round(pct_over_3_days, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(month) |>
  select(month, tests, median_days, pct_over_3_days)

turnaround
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Two arrow quirks worth knowing, both visible above

**`difftime()` only does seconds.** Ask arrow for any other unit and it
says so plainly: `difftime() with units other than secs not supported in
Arrow`. Take the seconds and convert to days after `collect()` — that
conversion is arithmetic on eighteen rows of summary, so it costs
nothing.

**The duration it hands back is not a number yet.** `as.numeric()` on it
fails with `Unsupported cast from duration[s] to double`, because arrow's
type system treats a duration as its own thing. `cast(x, int64())` — an
arrow function, not a dplyr one — is the conversion that works. This is
the seam where you stop writing portable dplyr and start writing arrow,
and it is worth noticing when you cross it.

**`median()` is approximate.** Run this query and arrow tells you:
`median() currently returns an approximate median in Arrow`. It uses a
streaming sketch rather than sorting every value, which is exactly what
lets it work on data larger than memory. For monitoring turnaround that
is fine. For a median that will be quoted in a publication, push the
query through `to_duckdb()` instead.
:::

There it is. Turnaround holds under a day through the quiet summer of
2020, then stretches as testing volume climbs into the winter surge —
the exact weeks the Commissioner is being briefed on. When labs are
busiest, results arrive slowest, so the most recent days in any report
are the *least* complete. Brief a count for the last three days during a
surge and you are briefing a number that is guaranteed to go up.

```{r}
#| label: turnaround-plot
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of median laboratory turnaround time by month, rising during the winter 2020-2021 surge."
turnaround |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = median_days)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Lab turnaround stretches exactly when it matters",
    subtitle = "Median days from specimen collection to result, synthetic feed",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median days"
  ) +
  theme_ct_horizontal()
```

## Step 4 — Why the numbers keep changing, part two: corrections

Lag isn't the whole story. Labs also **correct** results they have
already sent. In HL7, `result_status` carries `F` for final, `P` for
preliminary, and `C` for corrected.

```{r}
#| label: statuses
lab_ds |>
  group_by(result_status) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  collect() |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

Every `C` is a result that was already counted once, under a different
answer. Because corrections are a small slice, this is a case where
pulling them into R is the right call — `collect()` here is cheap:

```{r}
#| label: corrections
corrections <-
  lab_ds |>
  filter(result_status == "C") |>
  select(specimen_id, performing_lab, result_dt, result_value) |>
  collect()

# Which specimens came back with a *different* answer than before?
changed <-
  lab_ds |>
  select(specimen_id, result_value) |>
  collect() |>
  summarise(versions = n_distinct(result_value), .by = specimen_id) |>
  filter(versions > 1)

tibble(
  corrected_results = nrow(corrections),
  of_which_changed_the_answer = nrow(changed)
)
```

A few hundred corrections, and a quarter of them flipped the result. That
is the honest answer to the Commissioner's first question: **the numbers
change because the underlying results change**, partly by arriving late
and partly by being revised.

Which means a count of results is not the same as a count of specimens:

```{r}
#| label: dedupe
# One row per specimen: the most recent result wins.
deduped <-
  lab_ds |>
  select(specimen_id, result_dt, result_snomed) |>
  collect() |>
  slice_max(result_dt, n = 1, by = specimen_id, with_ties = FALSE)

tibble(
  rows_in_feed = nrow(lab_ds),
  distinct_specimens = nrow(deduped),
  difference = nrow(lab_ds) - nrow(deduped)
)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Deduplicate, don't drop

The tempting shortcut is `filter(result_status != "C")` — throw the
corrections away. That gets you the right row *count* and the wrong
*answers*, because you have just kept the superseded version of every
corrected result. Keep the latest, not the first.
:::

## Step 5 — Positivity, by method

The second question. Now it's a query against the dataset, and the
denominator comes with it:

```{r}
#| label: positivity
positivity <-
  lab_ds |>
  filter(!is.na(specimen_collection_dt)) |>
  mutate(is_positive = result_snomed %in% POSITIVE_CODES) |>
  group_by(collection_year, collection_month, test_method) |>
  summarise(tests = n(), positives = sum(is_positive), .groups = "drop") |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(
    month = make_date(collection_year, collection_month, 1),
    positivity = round(100 * positives / tests, 1)
  ) |>
  arrange(month, test_method)

positivity |>
  filter(month >= as.Date("2020-11-01"), month <= as.Date("2021-02-01"))
```

```{r}
#| label: positivity-plot
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of monthly test positivity split by test method."
positivity |>
  filter(test_method != "Chemiluminescent immunoassay") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = positivity, color = test_method)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "One positivity rate hides three different tests",
    subtitle = "Monthly positivity by test method, synthetic feed",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Positivity (%)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_ct_horizontal()
```

Serology is left out of that chart on purpose, and the reason is
epidemiology rather than code: an antibody test tells you about past
infection, so pooling it into a current-positivity number would inflate
the rate and mean nothing. It stays in the table, out of the trend.

That is the answer to the second question: no, it is not the same eleven
percent. Rapid antigen runs consistently below the amplification tests on
the same days, so a rising share of antigen testing pushes the blended
rate down even when nothing about transmission has changed.

## Step 6 — Save what the brief needs

The brief doesn't need the dataset. It needs two small tables and two
figures.

```{r}
#| label: save-outputs
#| eval: false
write_csv(positivity, here("outputs", "tables", "positivity_by_method.csv"))
write_csv(turnaround, here("outputs", "tables", "lab_turnaround.csv"))

ggsave(
  here("outputs", "figures", "positivity_by_method.png"),
  width = 8,
  height = 4.5,
  dpi = 300
)
```

## Step 7 — Into the brief

Add a section to `docs/situation-brief.qmd`. The point of it is the
caveat, not the chart — a number the Commissioner knows is provisional is
worth more than one they find out was provisional later.

````{verbatim}
#| lang: markdown
## Testing and data completeness

```{r}
#| label: brief-testing
#| include: false
positivity <- readr::read_csv(here("outputs", "tables", "positivity_by_method.csv"))
turnaround <- readr::read_csv(here("outputs", "tables", "lab_turnaround.csv"))

latest_tat <- dplyr::slice_max(turnaround, month, n = 1)
```

`r glue::glue("Results currently take a median of {latest_tat$median_days} days from collection to report, and {latest_tat$pct_over_3_days}% take longer than three days. Counts for the last several days are provisional and will rise.")`

![](../outputs/figures/positivity_by_method.png)

Positivity is reported by test method. Rapid antigen and amplification
tests are not interchangeable, and the share of testing done by each has
shifted over time — a change in the blended rate is not by itself a
change in transmission.
````

## Putting it together

```{r}
#| eval: false

# === setup ===
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(arrow)
library(fs)
library(lubridate)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
library(here)

# === constants ===
RAW_CSV <- here("data", "raw", "synthetic-covid-lab-results.csv")
LAB_DATASET <- here("data", "processed", "lab-results")
POSITIVE_CODES <- c("260373001", "10828004")

# === functions ===
convert_feed <- function(csv_path, dataset_path) {
  # Convert the raw ELR csv export into a partitioned parquet dataset.
  # Run this when new data arrives, not on every analysis.

  read_csv(
    csv_path,
    col_types = cols(
      result_snomed = col_character(),
      specimen_source_snomed = col_character(),
      ordering_provider_npi = col_character(),
      patient_zip = col_character(),
      .default = col_guess()
    )
  ) |>
    mutate(
      performing_lab = str_to_title(performing_lab),
      collection_year = year(specimen_collection_dt),
      collection_month = month(specimen_collection_dt)
    ) |>
    write_dataset(
      path = dataset_path,
      format = "parquet",
      partitioning = c("collection_year", "collection_month")
    )

  invisible(dataset_path)
}

lab_turnaround <- function(dataset) {
  # Median and tail of specimen-collection-to-result time, by month.

  dataset |>
    filter(!is.na(specimen_collection_dt)) |>
    mutate(
      # arrow does difftime in seconds only, and returns a duration
      # that needs cast() rather than as.numeric().
      turnaround_secs = cast(
        difftime(result_dt, specimen_collection_dt, units = "secs"),
        int64()
      )
    ) |>
    group_by(collection_year, collection_month) |>
    summarise(
      tests = n(),
      median_secs = median(turnaround_secs),
      pct_over_3_days = 100 * mean(turnaround_secs > 3 * 86400),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    collect() |>
    mutate(
      month = make_date(collection_year, collection_month, 1),
      median_days = round(median_secs / 86400, 1),
      pct_over_3_days = round(pct_over_3_days, 1)
    ) |>
    arrange(month) |>
    select(month, tests, median_days, pct_over_3_days)
}

positivity_by_method <- function(dataset, positive_codes) {
  # Monthly test counts, positives, and positivity, split by test method.

  dataset |>
    filter(!is.na(specimen_collection_dt)) |>
    mutate(is_positive = result_snomed %in% positive_codes) |>
    group_by(collection_year, collection_month, test_method) |>
    summarise(tests = n(), positives = sum(is_positive), .groups = "drop") |>
    collect() |>
    mutate(
      month = make_date(collection_year, collection_month, 1),
      positivity = round(100 * positives / tests, 1)
    ) |>
    arrange(month, test_method)
}

# === main ===
main <- function(refresh = FALSE) {
  # main entrypoint into our analysis
  #
  # refresh: logical - re-convert the raw csv before querying

  if (refresh || !dir_exists(LAB_DATASET)) {
    convert_feed(RAW_CSV, LAB_DATASET)
  }

  lab_ds <- open_dataset(LAB_DATASET)

  turnaround <- lab_turnaround(lab_ds)
  positivity <- positivity_by_method(lab_ds, POSITIVE_CODES)

  write_csv(turnaround, here("outputs", "tables", "lab_turnaround.csv"))
  write_csv(positivity, here("outputs", "tables", "positivity_by_method.csv"))

  positivity |>
    filter(test_method != "Chemiluminescent immunoassay") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = month, y = positivity, color = test_method)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    labs(
      title = "One positivity rate hides three different tests",
      x = NULL,
      y = "Positivity (%)",
      color = NULL
    )

  ggsave(
    here("outputs", "figures", "positivity_by_method.png"),
    width = 8,
    height = 4.5,
    dpi = 300
  )

  invisible(list(turnaround = turnaround, positivity = positivity))
}

# === entrypoint ===
main()
```

Note what `main()` does on a normal day: it does **not** re-convert
anything. The parquet dataset is already there, so the analysis opens it
and runs. Conversion is a separate branch, taken when the data is new.
That split — expensive once, cheap forever after — is the whole shape of
working with data too big to re-read.

## What's still manual

- The conversion runs against a CSV somebody still downloads. Chapter by
  chapter this project has been closing that kind of gap; the same
  `fetch_all_data()` idea from the APIs part applies here.
- `convert_feed()` rewrites the entire dataset every time. For a feed
  that only ever gains new months, rewriting the 2020 partitions is
  wasted work — writing just the new partitions is the natural next step.
- Nothing here checks that the file it was handed is the file it
  expected. A column quietly renamed upstream would sail straight
  through.
- The dedupe in Step 4 collects two columns for every row. That is fine
  at this size and would not be fine at sixteen million. That query needs
  a window function, which arrow's engine does not have — it is the
  opening problem of [the next chapter](duckdb.qmd).
